claims.text: The nanoparticles initially form a single-phase solid solution with a homogeneous elemental distribution.
High configurational entropy favors a homogeneous solid-solution phase.
Temperature-induced atomic diffusion can drive phase separation in these nanoparticles.
At 473–673 K, kinetic barriers inhibit atomic rearrangement.
Inhibited atomic rearrangement at 473–673 K maintains structural and chemical uniformity.
At temperatures approaching 1923 K, increased atomic mobility overcomes kinetic barriers.
Atomic mobility at high temperature leads to segregation and structural evolution.
Differences in atomic interactions provide a driving force for phase separation.
At lower temperatures, configurational entropy stabilizes the solid solution by restricting atomic diffusion.
Differences in favorable bonding among constituent atoms can promote segregation when atomic mobility increases.
Atomic-size differences can promote segregation when atomic mobility increases.
Nanoparticles held under catalytic-temperature conditions will largely retain their initial homogeneous structure.
Nanoparticles exposed to thermoelectric-temperature conditions will develop phase-separated domains or altered elemental distributions relative to the initial baseline.
The predicted temperature-dependent behavior is expected when oxidation is prevented.
The particle size must be sufficient to permit observable atomic diffusion for the predicted behavior to be detected.
Extreme particle-size reduction can confound the predicted temperature-dependent behavior.
Uncontrolled surface reactions can confound the predicted temperature-dependent behavior.
